questions.q: What is the core principle behind federated identity (SAML/OIDC)?
options: Every application maintains its own independent password database
Federation requires disabling all MFA
The user's password is transmitted to every trusting system
Systems trust a common identity through signed assertions or tokens, without any system seeing the user's actual password
questions.explain: Federation works by an IdP vouching through a signed, cryptographically verifiable artifact — the SP never sees the user's actual password, only the signed claim.

questions.q: Mechanically, what does Salesforce do during a delegated-authentication login attempt?
options: It makes a real-time SOAP web service callout to a client-hosted endpoint, sending the username and password it collected on its own login form
It issues a SAML assertion to the client
It bypasses authentication entirely for trusted IP ranges
It redirects the user to an external IdP's login page
questions.explain: Delegated authentication has Salesforce collect the username and password on its own form, then call out to a client-hosted web service that validates them and returns true/false.

questions.q: What key security property does delegated authentication lack, compared to SAML/OIDC federation?
options: It cannot be disabled once enabled
It lacks nothing; it's equally secure
Salesforce actually handles the user's password in transit to the callout, unlike federation where Salesforce never sees the password
It lacks the ability to authenticate users at all
questions.explain: Because the user's password passes through Salesforce's login form on its way to the client's callout endpoint, Salesforce does briefly see the actual password — a property federation (SAML/OIDC) specifically avoids.

questions.q: Why has delegated authentication largely become a legacy approach?
options: Salesforce removed support for it entirely
It only works for Experience Cloud sites
It was never actually implemented by any Salesforce customer
It requires the client to build and indefinitely maintain a custom authentication web service, and doesn't naturally support modern MFA or social sign-on
questions.explain: The ongoing maintenance burden of a custom-hosted endpoint, combined with poor support for modern MFA and social login flows, makes delegated authentication a less attractive choice than SAML/OIDC federation for new designs.

questions.q: If an architect finds delegated authentication configured in an older client org today, what's the generally recommended posture?
options: Recognize it as a legacy configuration and consider migrating to federated SSO as a modernization opportunity
Immediately disable all logins for the org
Delegated authentication cannot coexist with any other login method, so nothing can be done
Leave it exactly as-is forever with no further consideration
questions.explain: Delegated authentication mostly shows up in legacy orgs; recognizing it and evaluating a migration to SAML/OIDC federation is a reasonable modernization recommendation, not something to assume must stay unchanged.
